items.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015
items.q: I don’t know if you’re familiar with him, he’s a comedian. He was the king of the malapropisms.

ctx.x: So if you don’t, does it constitute — you know this term “wrong note” I know is debatable. But if you were teaching a lesson and someone’s playing a note that really doesn’t quite belong and they’re not either justifying it or setting it up. Would you say to that student, “that could be done better,” or something?

Oh of course, yes. And I would say it’s not a wrong note but it’s a wrong way to play that note over that chord. You know there’s a certain way to get to that note. If you’re going to just go for it and have it sound really wrong, which a lot of great players have done, you’ve got to have some way to skillfully tell everybody you meant to do that and it wasn’t a mistake. And you have to have the presence of mind, you have to be able to do that, and you have to be relaxed not to do that, and you have to be…

When I listen to some, any number of people, I think of Dizzy Gillespie sometimes. And sometimes he plays something and I go my God, I never would have thought of that. And it’s until you maybe listen to it again, it didn’t sound right.
